fields.meta_title: Data Entry Automation That Checks Every Field | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Describe what your team retypes, and Emergent builds data entry automation that saves checked records to your database. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build Data Entry Automation That Ends the Retyping
fields.hero_description: Build data entry automation that turns incoming forms and scans into checked records in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What the App Does With Every Record
fields.features_subheading: Every value is checked against your rules before it is written, once, to each system that needs it.
fields.feature_1:
Fields pulled from any format

Reads values out of email bodies and PDF attachments, plus phone photos of paper forms. Each one lands in its own column, typed as a date or a number where the field calls for it.
fields.feature_2:
Checks you write in plain English

Tests each entry against rules your team now applies by eye, such as SKUs that must exist in your catalog. An entry that fails waits in a review queue with the reason shown.
fields.feature_3:
Unclear values shown to a person

Sends any value the AI reads with low confidence, such as a smudged digit on a photographed form, to a reviewer with the source image beside it. Clear values save without waiting.
fields.feature_4:
Duplicates caught before they exist

Searches existing contacts by email or account number before writing a new one. A match updates the entry already there, and the earlier values stay in its change history.
fields.feature_5:
One entry written to every system

Pushes each approved entry to your CRM and your accounting software through their APIs. When a system rejects a write, the log shows its error and the entry waits for a retry.
fields.feature_6:
Code your team can take over

Exports the whole app as code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. The intake rules and the review queue come with it, and your data stays in a database your team owns.

fields.usecase_heading: Data Entry Jobs Teams Hand Off First
fields.tab_content_1:
The sheet is filed before the van leaves

Ben Walsh photographs his inspection sheet for unit HV-2207 at the end of a service call. The app reads 11 fields into job JOB-4471 and checks the serial against the customer's equipment list. Ten fields save on their own. The suction pressure is smudged, and it goes to Hannah Cole in the office with the photo attached.
fields.tab_content_2:
Cost jumps over 8% wait for a buyer

Halden Tools emails a new price list each month, 1,240 SKUs in a spreadsheet attachment. The app matches every row to your product catalog by SKU. Three SKUs rose more than 8%. Those keep last month's cost until Tessa Lindgren in purchasing approves the change, and the other 1,237 update right away.
fields.tab_content_3:
One contact per person, however many cards come back

Reps at the booth photograph each business card on their phones. The app reads the name and email, then searches the CRM by email before creating anything. Marta Olsen of Brightline Freight is already a contact. Her card adds a note to that contact instead of a second one: met at booth 14, asked about cold storage.
fields.tab_content_4:
Type the new customer in once

Corvel Logistics signs its setup form, and the app writes all 18 fields once. It creates the company in HubSpot and the organization in your help desk. The QuickBooks customer waits: the tax ID has 8 digits, and an EIN has 9. Rosa Klein in finance gets a direct message to correct it, and the sync finishes when she does.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to set up data entry automation for one source, with checks on every field before anything is saved.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Find the data your team retypes
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 List each field and where it goes
fields.howto_step_1_des: List every place someone copies data by hand this month, such as order emails or a spreadsheet passed between teams. Note how many entries each source produces a week. Start with the busiest source that keeps the same layout most of the time.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Pull 20 recent examples of that source, and keep the messy ones: a crooked scan, a form with a blank field, an email with the order in an attachment. They become your test set and show Emergent what the app has to handle.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write down every field you need with its type and the column or system it belongs in. Mark the required ones. Emergent builds the database and the intake screen from that list, which makes it the closest thing your project has to a spec.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Write down the checks your team does without thinking: a total that must match its line items, a customer number that must already exist, a phone number with the right digit count. Decide what happens when one fails and who sees the record.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect the systems the data belongs in, such as your CRM or accounting software, through their APIs. Map each field once. Send one sample to each system first and confirm it lands in the right place before you run the full set.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Run the samples and fix misreads
fields.howto_step_6_des: Push all 20 samples through and compare every field with what a person would have typed. Where the app misreads or misfiles something, describe the fix in a prompt and run the set again until it comes back clean.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Go live with a review queue
fields.howto_step_7_des: Switch it on for new records, with low-confidence fields still going to a reviewer. Watch the queue for two weeks. As corrections drop, narrow what needs review, then move to the next source on your list.

This page shows four data entry jobs as working screens: a handwritten service sheet read into a job record with one unclear reading sent to the office, a supplier price list matched to the catalog with large cost jumps held, trade-show business cards checked against the CRM so a known contact gets a note instead of a duplicate, and one signed setup form written to three systems with a bad tax ID held. scope.evidence: H1 'Build Data Entry Automation That Ends the Retyping', meta title 'Data Entry Automation That Checks Every Field | Emergent' and hero 'Build data entry automation that turns incoming forms and scans into checked records in a database you own.' (107 chars) state the whole job; how-to description is one 113-char sentence.

intent.evidence: Informational SERP of explainers and extraction vendors: page gives the definition (FAQ 1), OCR vs extraction (FAQ 4), RPA (FAQ 9), tool groups (FAQ 6), accuracy (FAQ 7), a 7-step how-to ('Gather 20 real samples', 'Go live with a review queue') and four worked jobs.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: 'suction pressure is smudged', '1,240 SKUs in a spreadsheet attachment', 'an EIN has 9'. Table uses the hub default column (no variant exists for these competitors; noted).

openers.evidence: Every paragraph opens on a full sentence: 'Ben Walsh photographs his inspection sheet...', 'Halden Tools emails a new price list each month...', features open on verbs ('Reads', 'Tests', 'Sends', 'Searches', 'Pushes', 'Exports').

craft.evidence: Short varied sentences, one idea each: 'Ten fields save on their own.' 'Three SKUs rose more than 8%.' No tacked-on endings found (QC Q5 clean).

voice.evidence: Concrete, unglamorous detail reads operator-written: 'met at booth 14, asked about cold storage'; 'Leave the hardest cases, like faxed forms, for a second round.'

truth.evidence: FAQ 3 'Handwriting and judgment calls ... still need a person' contradicts tab 1, feature 3, the paperFieldForms mockup and tab_image_1 alt, which show a handwritten sheet read automatically with only the one smudged value sent to a person.

distinct.evidence: Four jobs (field sheets, supplier price lists, booth cards, account setup) are specific to retyping; no sibling primary (excel, invoice, document automation) in any heading; document and task automation only linked in FAQ.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic items, each answered in the first sentence ('Optical character recognition (OCR) turns an image of text into characters...'); hub link in item 2; sibling links document automation and task automation; F9 lines in items 6 and 7.

images.evidence: Briefs match copy on names and numbers: tab 1 '11 fields read' / '10 saved' / Hannah Cole; tab 2 '3 SKUs held' / '1,237 costs updated' / Tessa Lindgren; tab 3 'Met at booth 14'; tab 4 'Held: tax ID has 8 digits' / 'To Rosa Klein'. One hero each; engine gates I1/I4 pass.

findings.quote: Handwriting and judgment calls, like which of two addresses is current, still need a person. A good setup automates the first group and sends the second to a review queue.
findings.issue: The page contradicts itself on its own core story. FAQ 3 says handwriting needs a person and goes to a review queue, but the rest of the page shows handwriting read automatically with only low-confidence values going to a person: tab_content_1 'Ten fields save on their own. The suction pressure is smudged, and it goes to Hannah Cole'; feature_3 'such as a smudged digit on a photographed form ... Clear values save without waiting'; mockup paperFieldForms 'reads photos of our handwritten inspection sheets ... send any value read with low confidence to our office coordinator'; tab_image_1 alt 'A photographed handwritten inspection sheet is read into 11 fields'. FAQ 7 ('faint phone photos of handwriting' read less reliably) is consistent; FAQ 3 is the only field that breaks.
findings.fix: Rewrite only FAQ 3 so it agrees with tab 1, e.g. 'Typed forms and clean PDFs automate well because each field sits in a predictable place. Handwriting reads less reliably, so its unclear values go to a person, and judgment calls, like which of two addresses is current, still need one.' Keep the review-queue sentence about the unclear group only.
